It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Possessor of bounty" means possessor of wealth, independent of anyone who does not say "There is no god but God." 'Ikrimah said: "Possessor of bounty" means possessor of kindness (mann). Al-Jawhari said: *al-tawl* with a fatḥah is kindness; it is said from it: "he *tala* upon him," and "he *tatawwala* upon him," when he showed kindness to him. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "Possessor of bounty" means possessor of grace (tafaddul). Al-Mawardi said: The difference between kindness (mann) and grace (tafaddul) is that kindness is pardon for a sin, while grace is benevolence not owed. *Al-tawl* is derived from *al-tiwal* (length), as if He lengthened His favour to others, or because the duration of His favour is long.

"There is no deity except Him; to Him is the final return" means the place of return.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. He, glory be to Him, recorded disbelief against those who dispute about the signs of God. The intended meaning is disputing with falsehood, by criticising them, aiming to refute the truth and extinguish the light of God, the Exalted. This is shown by His saying: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood to refute by it the truth﴾ [Ghafir: 5]. As for disputing about them in order to clarify what is ambiguous in them, to resolve their difficulties, to contend with the scholars over deriving their meanings, and to refute the deviators with them and from them, that is the greatest struggle (jihad) in the way of God. This meaning has already been discussed under al-Baqarah, at His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], comprehensively.[[See vol. 3, p. 283 and following, first or second edition.]]

"So do not be deceived" (fa-la yaghrurraka). It is also read "fa-la yaghurrak." "Their movement" (taqallubuhum) means their going about, "throughout the land" (fi al-bilad). For if I give them respite, I do not neglect them; rather I punish them. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means their trade from Mecca to Syria and to Yemen. It has also been said: "So do not be deceived" by what they have of good and abundance of provision, for it is a little enjoyment in this world. Al-Zajjaj said: "So do not be deceived" by their safety after their disbelief, for their end is destruction. Abu al-'Aliyah said: There are two verses most severe for those who dispute about the Qur'an: His saying, "None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve," and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme schism﴾ [al-Baqarah: 176].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verses 5–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied (the messengers)﴾, with the verb in the feminine form because the group is feminine, meaning: they denied the messengers. "And the factions after them": that is, the nations who formed factions against their prophets with denial, such as 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. "Every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him": that is, to imprison him and torment him. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: to kill him. The word "seize" (al-akhdh) is also used in the sense of destruction, as in His saying: ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My rejection?﴾ [al-Hajj: 44]. The Arabs call a captive "akhidh," because he is taken captive for killing. Qutrub recited the verse of the poet:

"Whether you seize me and kill me... how many a seizer desires my immortality"
[In the tafsir of al-Samin: "And how many a man desires my immortality."]

There are two views on when they seized their messenger: the first is when he invoked against them; the second is when the punishment descended upon them. "And they disputed with falsehood in order to refute the truth thereby": that is, to remove it. From this comes "a slippery place" (makan dahd), meaning a place where one slips. Falsehood is slippery (dahid), because it slides and does not hold firm. Yahya ibn Salam said: they disputed with the prophets using polytheism, in order to nullify faith thereby. "Then I seized them": that is, with punishment. "So how was My punishment?" meaning: what was the outcome for the nations that denied, i.e., did they not find it to be true?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus was the word of your Lord fulfilled﴾, meaning: it became obligatory and binding, derived from "truth" (al-haqq) because it is what is binding. "The word of your Lord": this is the reading of the majority in the singular. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "words" in the plural.

"Against those who disbelieved, that they": al-Akhfash said: that is, because they, and with them. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "innahum" with a kasra on the hamza. "Are the companions of the Fire": that is, those who are tormented in it. The sentence is complete. Then he began: "Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believed." It is related that the bearers of the Throne have their feet in the lowest earth and their heads have pierced the Throne, and they are humbly submissive, not raising their gaze. They are the noblest and most excellent of the angels. In a hadith (a report from the Prophet ﷺ): "Allah, blessed and exalted, commanded all the angels to send greetings of peace to the bearers of the Throne in the morning and evening, as a mark of their superiority over the rest of the angels." It is said: Allah created the Throne from a green jewel, and between its two legs, from its supports, the fluttering of a swiftly flying bird lasts eighty thousand years. It is also said: around the Throne are seventy thousand rows of angels who circle it, glorifying and exalting God, and behind them are seventy thousand rows standing, having placed their hands on their shoulders, raising their voices in glorification and exaltation, and behind them are a hundred thousand rows, having placed their right hands on their left; there is not one of them who does not glorify with something that the other does not glorify with.

Ibn Abbas read "al-'Urash" with a damma on the ayn. Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned all of this.

It is also said that this is connected with the mention of the disbelievers, because the meaning, and Allah knows best, is: "Those who bear the Throne and those around it" glorify Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, above what the disbelievers say, "and ask forgiveness for those who believed," that is, they ask Allah, may He be exalted, to forgive them.

The statements of the people of tafsir (exegesis) hold that the Throne is a throne-seat, that it is a formed body which Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, created, and commanded angels to bear it, and worshipped them by their exalting it and circling around it, just as He created on earth a House and commanded the children of Adam to circle it and face it in prayer.

Ibn Tahman narrated, from Musa ibn Uqbah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been permitted to narrate about an angel from among the angels of Allah, one of the bearers of the Throne, that the distance between the lobe of his ear and his shoulder is a journey of seven hundred years." Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it. It has already passed in al-Baqarah [See vol. 3, p. 276 and following, first or second edition], in the verse of the Throne (ayat al-Kursi), regarding the greatness of the Throne and that it is the greatest of created things.

Thawr ibn Yazid narrated, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, that he said: When Allah, may He be exalted, created the Throne, it said: "Allah will not create a creature greater than me." Then it trembled, so Allah encircled it with a serpent. The serpent has seventy thousand wings, on each wing seventy thousand feathers, on each feather seventy thousand faces, on each face seventy thousand mouths, and in each mouth seventy thousand tongues. From their mouths there comes out every day glorification equal in number to the drops of rain, the leaves of trees, the pebbles and the dust, the days of this world, and all the angels together. The serpent then coiled around the Throne, so the Throne reaches to the middle of the serpent, which is coiled around it.
[This report and similar ones are among the Isra'iliyat (narratives of Israelite origin) which storytellers bring in, and they are not authentically established.]

Mujahid said: between the seventh heaven and the Throne are seventy thousand veils, a veil of light and a veil of darkness, a veil of light and a veil of darkness.

"Our Lord": that is, they say: "Our Lord, You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge." That is: Your mercy and Your knowledge have encompassed everything. When the verb was transferred from the mercy and knowledge, it was put in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). "So forgive those who repented": that is, from polytheism and sins. "And followed Your way": that is, the religion of Islam. "And protect them from the punishment of Hellfire": that is, turn it away from them so that it does not reach them.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: The companions of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) used to say: the angels are better than Ibn al-Kawwa'. They ask forgiveness for those on earth, while Ibn al-Kawwa' bears witness against them of disbelief. Ibrahim said: They used to say that they do not withhold the seeking of forgiveness from anyone among the people of the qiblah.

Mutarrif ibn Abdullah said: We found that the most sincere of Allah's servants toward Allah's servants are the angels, and we found that the most deceitful of Allah's servants toward Allah's servants is Satan, and he recited this verse.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said to his companions regarding this verse: Understand it, for there is no shield in the world more hopeful than it. If a single angel were to ask Allah to forgive all the believers, He would forgive them. How much more so when all the angels and the bearers of the Throne ask forgiveness for the believers.

Khalaf ibn Hisham al-Bazzar al-Qari said: I was reading to Sulaym ibn Isa, and when I reached "and ask forgiveness for those who believed," he wept, then said: O Khalaf, how honored is the believer with Allah, sleeping on his bed while the angels ask forgiveness for him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden﴾. It is related that Umar ibn al-Khattab said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: What are the Gardens of Eden? He said: They are palaces of gold in Paradise, which the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the leaders of justice will enter. "Which You have promised them": "which" is in the accusative position as a qualifier of "gardens." "And those who were righteous": "those who" is in the accusative position, coordinated with the pronoun of "them" in His saying "admit them." "And those who were righteous" among "their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants," by faith. The likeness of this verse has already passed in al-Ra'd [See vol. 9, p. 312, first or second edition].

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man enters Paradise and says: "O Lord, where are my father, my grandfather, my mother? Where are my children and my children's children? Where are my wives?" It is said to him: "They did not do deeds like yours." He says: "O Lord, I was doing deeds for myself and for them." It is said: "Admit them into Paradise." Then he recited: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and those who were righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants﴾.

Close to this verse is His saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith, We will join them with their descendants﴾ [al-Tur: 21].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾. Qatadah said: that is, protect them from what would harm them. It was also said: the implied meaning is "protect them from the punishment of evil deeds." This is an imperative from "waqaahu Allah, yaqihi, wiqayah" (with a kasra), meaning He guarded him. ﴿And whoever is protected from evil deeds on that Day, You have indeed shown him mercy﴾, that is, by entering Paradise. ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, that is, the great salvation.

"Which You have promised them": "which" is in the accusative position as a qualifier of "gardens." "And those who were righteous": "those who" is in the accusative position, coordinated with the pronoun of "them" in His saying "admit them." "And those who were righteous" among "their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants," by faith. The likeness of this verse has already passed in al-Ra'd [See vol. 9, p. 312, first or second edition].

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man enters Paradise and says: "O Lord, where are my father, my grandfather, my mother? Where are my children and my children's children? Where are my wives?" It is said to him: "They did not do deeds like yours." He says: "O Lord, I was doing deeds for myself and for them." It is said: "Admit them into Paradise." Then he recited: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and those who were righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants﴾.

Close to this verse is His saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith, We will join them with their descendants﴾ [al-Tur: 21].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾. Qatadah said: that is, protect them from what would harm them. It was also said: the implied meaning is "protect them from the punishment of evil deeds." This is an imperative from "waqaahu Allah, yaqihi, wiqayah" (with a kasra), meaning He guarded him. ﴿And whoever is protected from evil deeds on that Day, You have indeed shown him mercy﴾, that is, by entering Paradise. ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, that is, the great salvation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verses 5–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied (the messengers)﴾, with the verb in the feminine form because the group is feminine, meaning: they denied the messengers. "And the factions after them": that is, the nations who formed factions against their prophets with denial, such as 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. "Every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him": that is, to imprison him and torment him. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: to kill him. The word "seize" (al-akhdh) is also used in the sense of destruction, as in His saying: ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My rejection?﴾ [al-Hajj: 44]. The Arabs call a captive "akhidh," because he is taken captive for killing. Qutrub recited the verse of the poet:

"Whether you seize me and kill me... how many a seizer desires my immortality"
[In the tafsir of al-Samin: "And how many a man desires my immortality."]

There are two views on when they seized their messenger: the first is when he invoked against them; the second is when the punishment descended upon them. "And they disputed with falsehood in order to refute the truth thereby": that is, to remove it. From this comes "a slippery place" (makan dahd), meaning a place where one slips. Falsehood is slippery (dahid), because it slides and does not hold firm. Yahya ibn Salam said: they disputed with the prophets using polytheism, in order to nullify faith thereby. "Then I seized them": that is, with punishment. "So how was My punishment?" meaning: what was the outcome for the nations that denied, i.e., did they not find it to be true?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus was the word of your Lord fulfilled﴾, meaning: it became obligatory and binding, derived from "truth" (al-haqq) because it is what is binding. "The word of your Lord": this is the reading of the majority in the singular. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "words" in the plural.

"Against those who disbelieved, that they": al-Akhfash said: that is, because they, and with them. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "innahum" with a kasra on the hamza. "Are the companions of the Fire": that is, those who are tormented in it. The sentence is complete. Then he began: "Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believed." It is related that the bearers of the Throne have their feet in the lowest earth and their heads have pierced the Throne, and they are humbly submissive, not raising their gaze. They are the noblest and most excellent of the angels. In a hadith (a report from the Prophet ﷺ): "Allah, blessed and exalted, commanded all the angels to send greetings of peace to the bearers of the Throne in the morning and evening, as a mark of their superiority over the rest of the angels." It is said: Allah created the Throne from a green jewel, and between its two legs, from its supports, the fluttering of a swiftly flying bird lasts eighty thousand years. It is also said: around the Throne are seventy thousand rows of angels who circle it, glorifying and exalting God, and behind them are seventy thousand rows standing, having placed their hands on their shoulders, raising their voices in glorification and exaltation, and behind them are a hundred thousand rows, having placed their right hands on their left; there is not one of them who does not glorify with something that the other does not glorify with.

Ibn Abbas read "al-'Urash" with a damma on the ayn. Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned all of this.

It is also said that this is connected with the mention of the disbelievers, because the meaning, and Allah knows best, is: "Those who bear the Throne and those around it" glorify Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, above what the disbelievers say, "and ask forgiveness for those who believed," that is, they ask Allah, may He be exalted, to forgive them.

The statements of the people of tafsir (exegesis) hold that the Throne is a throne-seat, that it is a formed body which Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, created, and commanded angels to bear it, and worshipped them by their exalting it and circling around it, just as He created on earth a House and commanded the children of Adam to circle it and face it in prayer.

Ibn Tahman narrated, from Musa ibn Uqbah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been permitted to narrate about an angel from among the angels of Allah, one of the bearers of the Throne, that the distance between the lobe of his ear and his shoulder is a journey of seven hundred years." Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it. It has already passed in al-Baqarah [See vol. 3, p. 276 and following, first or second edition], in the verse of the Throne (ayat al-Kursi), regarding the greatness of the Throne and that it is the greatest of created things.

Thawr ibn Yazid narrated, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, that he said: When Allah, may He be exalted, created the Throne, it said: "Allah will not create a creature greater than me." Then it trembled, so Allah encircled it with a serpent. The serpent has seventy thousand wings, on each wing seventy thousand feathers, on each feather seventy thousand faces, on each face seventy thousand mouths, and in each mouth seventy thousand tongues. From their mouths there comes out every day glorification equal in number to the drops of rain, the leaves of trees, the pebbles and the dust, the days of this world, and all the angels together. The serpent then coiled around the Throne, so the Throne reaches to the middle of the serpent, which is coiled around it.
[This report and similar ones are among the Isra'iliyat (narratives of Israelite origin) which storytellers bring in, and they are not authentically established.]

Mujahid said: between the seventh heaven and the Throne are seventy thousand veils, a veil of light and a veil of darkness, a veil of light and a veil of darkness.

"Our Lord": that is, they say: "Our Lord, You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge." That is: Your mercy and Your knowledge have encompassed everything. When the verb was transferred from the mercy and knowledge, it was put in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). "So forgive those who repented": that is, from polytheism and sins. "And followed Your way": that is, the religion of Islam. "And protect them from the punishment of Hellfire": that is, turn it away from them so that it does not reach them.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: The companions of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) used to say: the angels are better than Ibn al-Kawwa'. They ask forgiveness for those on earth, while Ibn al-Kawwa' bears witness against them of disbelief. Ibrahim said: They used to say that they do not withhold the seeking of forgiveness from anyone among the people of the qiblah.

Mutarrif ibn Abdullah said: We found that the most sincere of Allah's servants toward Allah's servants are the angels, and we found that the most deceitful of Allah's servants toward Allah's servants is Satan, and he recited this verse.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said to his companions regarding this verse: Understand it, for there is no shield in the world more hopeful than it. If a single angel were to ask Allah to forgive all the believers, He would forgive them. How much more so when all the angels and the bearers of the Throne ask forgiveness for the believers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 10–12:

His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called out to: The aversion of Allah towards you is greater than your aversion towards yourselves" (40:10). Al-Akhfash said: the *lam* in "lamaqtu" is the *lam* of inception (lam al-ibtida'), and it occurs after "yunadawna" (they will be called out) because its meaning is "it will be said to them," and calling out (al-nida') is a form of speech. Others said: the meaning is that it will be said to them: "The aversion of Allah towards you in the world, when you were being invited to faith and you disbelieved, is greater than the aversion of some of you towards others on the Day of Resurrection, because some of them were hostile to others and loathed them on the Day of Resurrection. So at that point they submitted, humbled themselves, and sought to leave the Fire." Al-Kalbi said: every person among the people of the Fire will say to himself, "I loathe you, O self," and the angels will say to them while they are in the Fire: "The aversion of Allah towards you when you were in the world, when messengers had been sent to you and you did not believe, is greater than your aversion towards yourselves today." Al-Hasan said: they will be given their books, and when they look at their evil deeds they will loathe themselves, and then they will be called out: "The aversion of Allah" towards you in the world, "when you were being invited to faith and you disbelieved," "is greater than your aversion towards yourselves" today. Mujahid said the same. Qatadah said: the meaning is: "The aversion of Allah" towards you "when you were being invited to faith and you disbelieved" "is greater than your aversion towards yourselves" when you witnessed the Fire. If it is asked: how is it valid that they loathe themselves? There are two answers. The first is that they placed themselves, through their sins, in the position of the loathed. The second is that when they came to a state in which desire had departed from them, and they knew that their own souls were what kept them in sins, they loathed them.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: when the people of the Fire despaired of what was with the guardians (al-khazana), and Malik said to them, "Indeed you will remain" (43:77), in what is coming, some of them said to others: "O people, there has come upon you of punishment and affliction what you see. Come, let us be patient; perhaps patience will benefit us, as the people of obedience were patient in obeying Allah and patience benefited them when they were patient." So they resolved together to be patient, and they were patient and their patience lasted long. Then they became impatient and called out: "Whether we are impatient or patient, it is the same for us; there is no refuge for us" (14:21), that is, no shelter. Then Iblis said at that point: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. I had no authority over you..." (14:22), up to His saying: "I cannot help you, nor can you help me" (14:22), meaning: I cannot benefit you in anything. "Indeed I disbelieved in what you associated with Allah before" (14:22). So when they heard his words, they loathed themselves. He said: then they were called out: "The aversion of Allah towards you is greater than your aversion towards yourselves, when you were being invited to faith and you disbelieved" (40:10), up to His saying: "Is there any way out?" (40:11). He said: then it was answered them: "That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, and if partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great" (40:12). Ibn al-Mubarak recorded this.

His saying, exalted is He: "They will say: Our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice" (40:11). The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of their saying, "You made us die twice and gave us life twice." Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: they were dead in the loins of their fathers; then He gave them life, then He caused them to die the death that is unavoidable in the world, then He gave them life for resurrection and the Last Day. Thus these are two lives and two deaths, and this is His saying: "How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then give you life again" (2:28). Al-Suddi said: they were made to die in the world, then He gave them life in the graves for questioning, then they were made to die and then given life in the Hereafter. He arrived at this only because the word "dead" (mayyit) in custom does not apply to a drop of semen. The scholars derived from this the proof for the questioning in the grave; for if reward and punishment were for the spirit alone and not the body, what would be the meaning of giving life and causing death? The spirit, according to those who restrict the rulings of the Hereafter to spirits, does not die, does not change, and does not decay; it is alive in itself, and neither death nor unconsciousness nor annihilation reaches it. Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying, "Our Lord, You have made us die twice..." up to the end of the verse: He created them in the back of Adam, brought them out, gave them life, took their covenant, then caused them to die, then gave them life in the world, then caused them to die. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 1 p. 249, second or third edition]]. "So we have acknowledged our sins": they acknowledged where acknowledgment would not benefit them, and they regretted where regret would not benefit them. "Is there any way out?" That is: can we be returned to the world so that we may act in obedience to You? Its parallel is: "Is there any way of return?" (42:44), and His saying: "Return us, and we will do righteous deeds" (32:12), and His saying: "If only we could be returned" (6:27), up to the end of the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: "That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved" (40:12). "That" (dhalikum) is in the nominative position, meaning: the matter is that (dhalikum), or "that" (dhalikumu) is the punishment you are in, because of your disbelief. In the speech there is an omitted element whose implied sense is: they were answered that there is no way to return. That is because "when Allah was invoked," meaning when Allah was made One, "alone, you disbelieved" and denied that divinity belongs to Him exclusively; but if a associator associated partners with Him, you confirmed him and believed his words. Al-Tha'labi said: I heard some scholars say: "If partners are associated with Him" after the return to the world, if (the associator) were with Him, "you would believe," meaning you would confirm the associator; its parallel is: "Even if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden" (6:28). "So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great," exalted above having a consort or a son.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: when the people of the Fire despaired of what was with the guardians (al-khazana), and Malik said to them, "Indeed you will remain" (43:77), in what is coming, some of them said to others: "O people, there has come upon you of punishment and affliction what you see. Come, let us be patient; perhaps patience will benefit us, as the people of obedience were patient in obeying Allah and patience benefited them when they were patient." So they resolved together to be patient, and they were patient and their patience lasted long. Then they became impatient and called out: "Whether we are impatient or patient, it is the same for us; there is no refuge for us" (14:21), that is, no shelter. Then Iblis said at that point: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. I had no authority over you..." (14:22), up to His saying: "I cannot help you, nor can you help me" (14:22), meaning: I cannot benefit you in anything. "Indeed I disbelieved in what you associated with Allah before" (14:22). So when they heard his words, they loathed themselves. He said: then they were called out: "The aversion of Allah towards you is greater than your aversion towards yourselves, when you were being invited to faith and you disbelieved" (40:10), up to His saying: "Is there any way out?" (40:11). He said: then it was answered them: "That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, and if partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great" (40:12). Ibn al-Mubarak recorded this.

His saying, exalted is He: "They will say: Our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice" (40:11). The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of their saying, "You made us die twice and gave us life twice." Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: they were dead in the loins of their fathers; then He gave them life, then He caused them to die the death that is unavoidable in the world, then He gave them life for resurrection and the Last Day. Thus these are two lives and two deaths, and this is His saying: "How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then give you life again" (2:28). Al-Suddi said: they were made to die in the world, then He gave them life in the graves for questioning, then they were made to die and then given life in the Hereafter. He arrived at this only because the word "dead" (mayyit) in custom does not apply to a drop of semen. The scholars derived from this the proof for the questioning in the grave; for if reward and punishment were for the spirit alone and not the body, what would be the meaning of giving life and causing death? The spirit, according to those who restrict the rulings of the Hereafter to spirits, does not die, does not change, and does not decay; it is alive in itself, and neither death nor unconsciousness nor annihilation reaches it. Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying, "Our Lord, You have made us die twice..." up to the end of the verse: He created them in the back of Adam, brought them out, gave them life, took their covenant, then caused them to die, then gave them life in the world, then caused them to die. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 1 p. 249, second or third edition]]. "So we have acknowledged our sins": they acknowledged where acknowledgment would not benefit them, and they regretted where regret would not benefit them. "Is there any way out?" That is: can we be returned to the world so that we may act in obedience to You? Its parallel is: "Is there any way of return?" (42:44), and His saying: "Return us, and we will do righteous deeds" (32:12), and His saying: "If only we could be returned" (6:27), up to the end of the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: "That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved" (40:12). "That" (dhalikum) is in the nominative position, meaning: the matter is that (dhalikum), or "that" (dhalikumu) is the punishment you are in, because of your disbelief. In the speech there is an omitted element whose implied sense is: they were answered that there is no way to return. That is because "when Allah was invoked," meaning when Allah was made One, "alone, you disbelieved" and denied that divinity belongs to Him exclusively; but if a associator associated partners with Him, you confirmed him and believed his words. Al-Tha'labi said: I heard some scholars say: "If partners are associated with Him" after the return to the world, if (the associator) were with Him, "you would believe," meaning you would confirm the associator; its parallel is: "Even if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden" (6:28). "So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great," exalted above having a consort or a son.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verses 13-17:

﴿He is the One who shows you His signs﴾: that is, the proofs of His oneness and His power. "And sends down for you provision from the sky": He combined the showing of the signs and the sending down of provision, because the bodies are sustained by the signs and the bodies are sustained by provision. These signs are the heavens and the earths, what is in them and what is between them, including the sun, the moon, the stars, the winds, the clouds, the vapour, the rivers, the springs, the mountains, the trees, and the traces of peoples who were destroyed. "And none remembers": that is, none takes admonition from these signs so as to affirm the oneness of Allah, "except one who turns back" in repentance, that is, who returns to obedience to Allah. "So call upon Allah": that is, worship Him, "sincere in religion for Him": that is, in worship. It was also said: in obedience. "Though the disbelievers dislike it": the worship of Allah, so do not you worship anything other than Him.

﴿Raised in degrees, Lord of the Throne﴾: "Lord of the Throne" is in the nominative by implying a subject. Al-Akhfash said: it is also permissible to put it in the accusative as a form of praise. The meaning of "Raised in degrees" is "raised in attributes." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Raised of the seven heavens." Yahya ibn Sallam said: it refers to the elevation of the rank of His friends in Paradise, so "Raised" according to this view is in the sense of "one who raises," the form fa'il in the sense of fa'il. According to the first view it is one of the essential attributes, and its meaning is the One above whom there is no one higher in rank, and He is the one deserving the degrees of praise and commendation, which are their categories and their gates, and none deserves them but Him, said al-Halimi. We have mentioned this in the book al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna (al-Asna), and praise be to Allah. "Lord of the Throne": that is, its Creator and its Owner, not that He is in need of it. It was also said: this is from their saying "the throne of so-and-so was destroyed," meaning his kingship and his might ceased to exist. Thus "Lord of the Throne," glorified is He, means the permanence of His kingship and His authority, and we have explained this in al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna. "He casts the Spirit": that is, the revelation and prophethood, "upon whomever He wills of His servants." That is called "spirit" because people are given life by it, that is, they are brought to life from the death of disbelief, just as bodies are given life by spirits. Ibn Zayd said: the Spirit is the Qur'an. Allah, exalted is He, said: "And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command" (42:52). It was also said: the Spirit is Gabriel. Allah, exalted is He, said: "The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart" (26:193-194), and He said: "Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth" (16:102). "Of His command": that is, of His word. It was also said: of His decree. It was also said: "of" means "by," that is, by His command. "Upon whomever He wills of His servants": they are the prophets, and He wills that they be prophets, and no one has any will in this matter.

﴿To warn of the Day of Meeting﴾: that is, the Messenger is only sent to warn of the Day of Resurrection. So His saying "to warn" refers back to the Messenger. It was also said: "to warn" means that Allah, by sending the messengers to the creatures, warns "of the Day of Meeting." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayqa read "to warn" with the letter ta', addressing the Prophet, peace be upon him. "The Day of Meeting": Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: the day when the people of the heavens and the people of the earth meet. Qatada also said, as did Abu al-'Aliya and Muqatil: on it the creation and the Creator meet. It was also said: the worshippers and those worshipped. It was also said: the oppressor and the oppressed. It was also said: each person meets the reward of his deeds. It was also said: the first and the last meet on one level plain, a meaning reported from Ibn 'Abbas. All of these are correct in meaning.

﴿The Day they will come forth﴾: this may be a substitute for the first "Day." It was also said: "they" is in the nominative position as the subject, and "coming forth" is its predicate, and the clause is in the genitive position by annexation, which is why the tanwin is dropped from "Day." According to Sibawayh this happens when the time expression has the meaning of "when" (idh). You say: "I met you on the day Zayd is governor." If it has the meaning of "whenever" (idha), it is not permitted, as in: "I will meet you on the day Zayd is governor." The meaning of "coming forth" is going out from their graves, with nothing concealing them, because on that day the earth will be a level plain with no crookedness or elevation in it, as was explained earlier in Ta-Ha.

﴿Nothing of them is hidden from Allah﴾: it was said that this is the governing element for "the Day they will come forth," that is, nothing of them is hidden from Him, nor of their deeds, on the Day they come forth.

﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾: this is at the annihilation of creation. Al-Hasan said: He, exalted is He, is the Questioner and the Answerer, because He says this when no one is there to answer Him, so He answers Himself, glorified is He, saying: ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾. Al-Nahhas said: the most correct thing said about this is what Abu Wa'il reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The people will be gathered on a white earth like silver, on which Allah, mighty and majestic, has never been disobeyed. A herald will be commanded to call out: "Whose is the dominion today?" The servants, believers and disbelievers alike, will say: "To Allah, the One, the Subduer." The believers will give this answer with joy and delight, and the disbelievers will give it in grief, submission and humility. As for this happening while the creation does not exist, that is far-fetched, because there is no benefit in it. The report from Ibn Mas'ud is sound, and it is not something to be derived by analogy or interpreted.

I say: The first view is very evident, because the aim is to show that Allah, exalted is He, alone possesses the dominion, when the claims of claimants have ended and the affiliations of those who claimed kinship have ceased. Every king has gone with his kingdom, and every arrogant one with his dominion, and their lineages and claims have been cut off. This is indicated by His, the Truth's, saying when He seizes the earth and the spirits and folds up the heavens: "I am the King, where are the kings of the earth?" as was mentioned earlier in the hadith of Abu Hurayra and in the hadith of Ibn Umar. Then He folds the earth with His left hand and the heavens with His right hand, then says: "I am the King, where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?" And from him, glorified is He, is His saying: "Whose is the dominion today?" It is the cessation of the time of this world, and after it will come the Resurrection and the gathering. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: His saying, glorified is He, "Whose is the dominion today?" occurs between the two blasts, when creation has perished and only the Creator remains, so He sees no one other than Himself as owner or owned, and says: "Whose is the dominion today?" No one answers Him, because the creatures are dead, so He answers Himself: "To Allah, the One, the Subduer," because He remains alone and has subdued His creation. It was also said: a herald will call out: "Whose is the dominion today?" and the people of Paradise will answer him: "To Allah, the One, the Subduer." Allah knows best. This was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾: that is, it will be said to them, when they acknowledge that the dominion on that day belongs to Allah alone: "Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned," whether good or evil. "No injustice today": that is, no one will have anything of his deeds diminished. "Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning": that is, He does not need to think or count on His fingers as reckoners do, because He is the All-Knowing, from whose knowledge nothing is hidden, so He does not delay the reward of anyone because He is occupied with another. Just as He provides for them in a single moment, so He reckons them in a single moment. This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqara [see vol. 2, p. 435, second edition]. And in a report: "The day will not reach midday before the people of Paradise have taken their midday rest in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire."

"So call upon Allah": that is, worship Him, "sincere in religion for Him": that is, in worship. It was also said: in obedience. "Though the disbelievers dislike it": the worship of Allah, so do not you worship anything other than Him.

The meaning of "Raised in degrees" is "raised in attributes." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Raised of the seven heavens." Yahya ibn Sallam said: it refers to the elevation of the rank of His friends in Paradise, so "Raised" according to this view is in the sense of "one who raises," the form fa'il in the sense of fa'il. According to the first view it is one of the essential attributes, and its meaning is the One above whom there is no one higher in rank, and He is the one deserving the degrees of praise and commendation, which are their categories and their gates, and none deserves them but Him, said al-Halimi. We have mentioned this in the book al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna (al-Asna), and praise be to Allah. "Lord of the Throne": that is, its Creator and its Owner, not that He is in need of it. It was also said: this is from their saying "the throne of so-and-so was destroyed," meaning his kingship and his might ceased to exist. Thus "Lord of the Throne," glorified is He, means the permanence of His kingship and His authority, and we have explained this in al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna. "He casts the Spirit": that is, the revelation and prophethood, "upon whomever He wills of His servants." That is called "spirit" because people are given life by it, that is, they are brought to life from the death of disbelief, just as bodies are given life by spirits. Ibn Zayd said: the Spirit is the Qur'an. Allah, exalted is He, said: "And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command" (42:52). It was also said: the Spirit is Gabriel. Allah, exalted is He, said: "The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart" (26:193-194), and He said: "Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth" (16:102). "Of His command": that is, of His word. It was also said: of His decree. It was also said: "of" means "by," that is, by His command. "Upon whomever He wills of His servants": they are the prophets, and He wills that they be prophets, and no one has any will in this matter.

It was also said: "to warn" means that Allah, by sending the messengers to the creatures, warns "of the Day of Meeting." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayqa read "to warn" with the letter ta', addressing the Prophet, peace be upon him. "The Day of Meeting": Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: the day when the people of the heavens and the people of the earth meet. Qatada also said, as did Abu al-'Aliya and Muqatil: on it the creation and the Creator meet. It was also said: the worshippers and those worshipped. It was also said: the oppressor and the oppressed. It was also said: each person meets the reward of his deeds. It was also said: the first and the last meet on one level plain, a meaning reported from Ibn 'Abbas. All of these are correct in meaning.

﴿The Day they will come forth﴾: this may be a substitute for the first "Day." It was also said: "they" is in the nominative position as the subject, and "coming forth" is its predicate, and the clause is in the genitive position by annexation, which is why the tanwin is dropped from "Day." According to Sibawayh this happens when the time expression has the meaning of "when" (idh). You say: "I met you on the day Zayd is governor." If it has the meaning of "whenever" (idha), it is not permitted, as in: "I will meet you on the day Zayd is governor." The meaning of "coming forth" is going out from their graves, with nothing concealing them, because on that day the earth will be a level plain with no crookedness or elevation in it, as was explained earlier in Ta-Ha.

﴿Nothing of them is hidden from Allah﴾: it was said that this is the governing element for "the Day they will come forth," that is, nothing of them is hidden from Him, nor of their deeds, on the Day they come forth.

Al-Hasan said: He, exalted is He, is the Questioner and the Answerer, because He says this when no one is there to answer Him, so He answers Himself, glorified is He, saying: ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾. Al-Nahhas said: the most correct thing said about this is what Abu Wa'il reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The people will be gathered on a white earth like silver, on which Allah, mighty and majestic, has never been disobeyed. A herald will be commanded to call out: "Whose is the dominion today?" The servants, believers and disbelievers alike, will say: "To Allah, the One, the Subduer." The believers will give this answer with joy and delight, and the disbelievers will give it in grief, submission and humility. As for this happening while the creation does not exist, that is far-fetched, because there is no benefit in it. The report from Ibn Mas'ud is sound, and it is not something to be derived by analogy or interpreted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 18–22:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And warn them of the Approaching Day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. It is so called because it is near, since everything that is coming is near. One says "azifa fulan" meaning he drew near, yaʼzifu azafan. An-Nabigha said:

Departure has drawn near, though our mounts have not yet been loaded, while our state is what it is, and as if it had already come.

That is, it has drawn near. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿The Approaching [Hour] has drawn near﴾ [[Verse 57 of Surah an-Najm.]] [An-Najm: 57], meaning the Hour has drawn near. Some of them would recite and say:

Departure has drawn near, and I have no provision except sins, for my wretchedness and my adversity.

"When the hearts are at the throats, choking with grief" is a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is understood in terms of meaning. Az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that the hearts of people are "at the throats" in a state of choking. Al-Farra' permitted that the implied sense is "and warn them" while they are choking. He also permitted the nominative reading of "choking" as the predicate of "the hearts," and said: the meaning is "when they are choking." Al-Kisa'i said: it is permissible to read "choking" in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "the Day of the Approaching" is the day of the presence of death, as said by Qutrub, and likewise "when the hearts are at the throats" refers to the time of the presence of death. But the first view is more evident.

Qatadah said: fear has lodged in the throats, so they neither come out nor return to their places. This does not occur except on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: "and their hearts are a void." It has also been said that this is a report about the extreme of anguish, as He said: "and the hearts reached the throats." The day is attributed to "the Approaching" by way of the implied phrase "the Day of the Resurrection, the Approaching," or "the Day of the Dispute, the Approaching." According to the Kufans, this is of the type of attributing a thing to itself, like "masjid al-jami'" and "salat al-ula."

"The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who is obeyed," meaning no near friend who benefits, and no intercessor whose intercession is accepted on their behalf.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾. Al-Mu'arrij said: there is inversion in it, meaning He knows the treacherous eyes. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the man who sits with a people when a woman passes by, and he steals a glance at her. And from him: it is the man who looks at a woman, and when his companions look at him he lowers his gaze, and when he sees them heedless he peeks again with his glance, and when they look at him he lowers his gaze again; and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows of him that he would love to look at her private parts. Mujahid said: it is the stealing of glances of the eyes toward what Allah has forbidden. Qatadah said: it is the winking of the eye and its closing toward what Allah the Exalted does not love. Ad-Dahhak said: it is a person's saying "I did not see" when he has seen, or "I saw" when he did not see. As-Suddi said: it is signalling with the eye. Sufyan said: it is the glance following a glance. Al-Farra' said: "the treachery of the eyes" is the second glance, and "what the breasts conceal" is the first glance. Ibn 'Abbas said: "what the breasts conceal" means whether he would commit adultery with her if he were alone with her or not. It has also been said: "what the breasts conceal" is what they hide and harbour.

When 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), after the people of Makkah had been reassured and 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) had requested safe conduct for him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was silent for a long time, then said: "Yes." When he had departed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to those around him: "I was silent only so that one of you would stand up and strike his neck." The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 40, verses 23–27:

God's words: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs mentioned in His words: ﴿And We gave Musa nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra: 101]. Their identification has already been discussed [[See vol. 10, p. 335 and following, first or second edition.]]. "And a clear authority" means with clear, evident proof. It may be masculine or feminine. It was said that by "authority" is meant the Torah. "To Fir'awn (Pharaoh), Haman and Qarun." He singled them out because the planning against Musa centred on them. Fir'awn was the king, Haman was the vizier, and Qarun was the owner of wealth and treasures. God joined him with the two of them because his conduct in disbelief and denial was like theirs. "They said: a sorcerer, a liar." When they were unable to match him, they attributed the miracles to sorcery.

God's words: ﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us﴾, meaning the manifest miracle. "They said: Kill the sons of those who believed with him." Qatadah said: this killing was different from the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys after Musa's birth. When God sent Musa, they resumed the killing of the Children of Israel as a punishment for them, so that people would be deterred from faith, and so that their numbers would not grow and they would not be strengthened by their male offspring. God diverted them from this by what He sent down upon them of various kinds of punishment, such as the frogs, the lice, the blood and the flood, until they left Egypt, and God drowned them. This is the meaning of God's words: ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, meaning in loss and ruin. People are not deterred from faith even if such things are done to them, so his plotting goes to waste.

God's words: ﴿And Fir'awn said: Leave me, let me kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord﴾. "Aqtul" is in the jussive (jazm), because it is the answer to the imperative. "Wal-yad'u" is in the jussive, because it is an imperative. "Dharuni" is not jussive, even though it is an imperative, but its form is that of the jussive, and it is indeclinable (mabni). It was said: this indicates that Fir'awn was told, "We fear that he will call down a curse upon you and it will be answered," and so he said: ﴿let him call upon his Lord﴾, meaning, let not what is mentioned of his Lord frighten you, for it has no reality, and I am your Lord, the Most High. ﴿Indeed I fear that he will change your religion﴾, meaning your worship of me into the worship of his Lord, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾. ﴿If he does not change your religion, he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, meaning that dissension will arise among people because of him.

The reading of the people of Madinah, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr is: "aw an yuzhira fi al-ardi al-fasad" (with "aw" and "al-fasad" in the accusative). The reading of the Kufans is: "an yazhara al-fasadu" (with the yā' of "yazhara" vowelled with a fatha, and "al-fasadu" in the nominative), and so it is in the codices of the Kufans. **First question:** Concerning the verse, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And a believing man said﴾. Some exegetes (*tafsir*, explanation of the Qur'an) mentioned that the name of this man was Habib. It is also said that he was Shim'an, with a shin (ش). Al-Suhayli said: "This is the most sound of what has been said about him." In *Tarikh al-Tabari*, may Allah have mercy on him, his name is given as Khabarak. (In the margin of al-Tabari it is written "Habrak," and in another copy "Jabrak.") It is also said that he was Hizqil. Al-Tha'labi reported this from Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars. Al-Zamakhshari said: "His name is Sam'an or Habib." It is also said that he was Kharbil or Hizbil.

Scholars differ over whether he was of the Children of Israel or a Copt. Al-Hasan and others said he was a Copt. It is said that he was a paternal cousin of Pharaoh, as al-Suddi reported. Al-Suddi said: "He is the one who was saved along with Musa, peace be upon him. For this reason Allah says ﴿from the family of Pharaoh﴾." This man is the one meant by Allah's words: ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said: "O Musa..."﴾ [al-Qasas: 20]. This is the view of Muqatil.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "No believer from the family of Pharaoh existed apart from him, apart from Pharaoh's wife, and apart from the believer who warned Musa, saying: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ [al-Qasas: 20]."

It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The sincere truthful ones (*al-siddiqun*) are three: Habib the carpenter, the believer of the family of Ya-Sin, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh who said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?﴾ And the third is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and he is the best of them." [The addition was cited by al-Jamal in his commentary, from al-Qurtubi.]

In this there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: do not be surprised by the polytheists of your people.

This man had standing (*wajaha*) with Pharaoh, and for this reason no harm befell him. It is also said that this man was from the Children of Israel, concealing his faith from the family of Pharaoh, as al-Suddi also reported.

According to this view, the phrase ﴿from the family of Pharaoh﴾ is a delayed modifier (*taqdim* and *ta'khir*) of the word ﴿a man﴾. The meaning is: "And a believing man, attributed to the family of Pharaoh," that is, from his people and relatives. As for the one who considers him from the Children of Israel, then the phrase ﴿believing﴾ is connected to ﴿concealing﴾, and it stands in the position of the second object of *yaktumu* (he conceals).

Al-Qushayri said: "Whoever considers him from the Children of Israel has a weak reading, because one says *katamahu amra kadha* (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and one does not say *katama minhu* (he concealed from him). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah a statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]. Also, Pharaoh would not tolerate such a statement from the Children of Israel."

**Second question:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾. That is, *li-an yaqula* (because he says), and *min ajli an yaqula rabbiya Allah* (on account of his saying "My Lord is Allah"). The *an* here stands in the accusative position after the removal of the preposition.

﴿And he has certainly brought you clear evidences from your Lord﴾, meaning the nine signs. ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lying﴾. He did not say this out of doubt about Musa's messengership and truthfulness, but as a gentle means of persuading them to restrain themselves and to withdraw from harming him.

If it had been *wa-in yakun* (with the nun), it would have been permissible, and *lakum* would have dropped the nun due to frequent usage according to the opinion of Sibawayh, and because it is the nun of i'rab (grammatical inflection) according to the opinion of Abu al-'Abbas.

﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you﴾. That is: if he does not strike you except with some of what he promises you, you will be destroyed.

The position of Abu 'Ubaydah is that the meaning of ﴿some of what he promises you﴾ is "all of what he promises you." He recited the verse of Labid:

*Tarrāku amkinatin idhā lam arḍahā*
*aw yartabiṭ baʿḍa al-nufūsi ḥimāmuhā*
*(She abandons places when I am not pleased with them, or when the death of some souls is tied to them.)*
[It is narrated as "aw yaʿtaliq" instead of "yartabiṭ," as in Lisan al-'Arab and others.]

So *ba'd* here means *kull* (all), because when some of them are struck, the whole of them is necessarily struck, since they are included in the threat. This is a softening of speech in admonition.

Al-Mawardi mentioned that *al-ba'd* may be used in place of *al-kull* as gentleness in address and breadth in speech, as the poet said (he is 'Umar al-Qutami):

*Qad yudrik al-mutanni baʿḍa ḥājatihi*
*wa-qad yakūnu maʿa al-mutaʿajjili al-zalalu*
*(The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error.)*

It is also said: he said this because he warned them of kinds of punishment, each of which is destructive. So it is as if he warned them that some of those kinds would strike them. It is also said that Musa promised them the punishment of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter if they disbelieved; so the meaning is that one of the two punishments will strike you. It is also said: that is, this punishment which he speaks of will strike you in this world, and it is *some* of the threat, and then the punishment in the Hereafter follows in succession. It is also said: he promised them punishment if they disbelieved and reward if they believed, so when they disbelieve, some of what they were promised will strike them.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is extravagant﴾ against himself, ﴿a liar﴾ against his Lord. This is a reference to Musa, and this would be part of the believer's speech. It is also said: "extravagant" in his obstinacy and "a liar" in his claim; this is a reference to Pharaoh, and this would be the speech of Allah the Exalted.

**Third question:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿concealing his faith﴾. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: Some people supposed that if the responsible person conceals his faith and does not utter it with his tongue, he is not a believer in his belief. Malik said: If a man intends disbelief in his heart, he is a disbeliever even if he does not utter it with his tongue. As for when he intends faith in his heart, he is never a believer until he utters it with his tongue. Fear and taqiyya (concealment for protection) do not prevent him from uttering it with his tongue between himself and Allah the Exalted; they only prevent him from having others hear it. Hearing by others is not a condition of faith's validity as a obligation. Rather, others' hearing it is required only so that they may refrain from harming him and his property.

**Fourth question:** Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr who said: I said to 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "Tell me of the most severe thing the polytheists did to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt came, seized the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, twisted his garment around his neck, and choked him severely. Then Abu Bakr came, took hold of his shoulder, pushed him away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' and he has certainly brought you clear evidences from your Lord?﴾" This is the wording of al-Bukhari.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim recorded it in *Nawadir al-Usul* from the hadith of Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Quraysh gathered after the death of Abu Talib by three days, and they intended to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This one struck him [*yajuʾuhu*: he struck him; *al-talltala*: shaking, disturbing, and jolting] and that one shook him. So the Prophet ﷺ called for help that day, and no one came to his aid except Abu Bakr, who had two braids. He came striking this one and shaking that one, and he said with the highest of his voice: 'Woe to you! ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ By Allah, he is truly the Messenger of Allah!' That day one of Abu Bakr's two braids was cut off." 'Ali said: "By Allah, the day of Abu Bakr is better than the believer of the family of Pharaoh. That man concealed his faith, and Allah praised him in His Book, while this Abu Bakr manifested his faith and expended his wealth and his blood for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

I say: 'Ali's words, "that man concealed his faith," mean at the beginning of his affair, in contrast with the Siddiq, for he manifested his faith and did not conceal it. Otherwise, the Qur'an clearly states that the believer of the family of Pharaoh manifested his faith when they intended to kill Musa, peace be upon him, as will come in its explanation.

Also in *Nawadir al-Usul*, from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with her: they said to her, "What is the most severe thing you saw the polytheists inflict upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" She said: "The polytheists were sitting in the mosque discussing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and what he says about their gods. While they were like that, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered, and they all rose toward him. Whenever they asked him about something, he would tell them the truth. They said: 'Do you not say such-and-such about our gods?' He said: 'Yes.' Then they all seized him. The cry for help reached Abu Bakr, and someone said to him: 'Rescue your companion!' So he left us, and he had braids, and he entered the mosque saying: 'Woe to you! ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah," and he has certainly brought you clear evidences from your Lord?﴾' So they let go of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and turned upon Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr returned to us, and he would not touch any of his braids without it coming away with him, while he said: 'Blessed are You, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor, Honor, Honor!'"

By "the land" is meant the land of Egypt, according to al-Suddi and others, like His saying: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾ [Yusuf: 21], meaning in the land of Egypt. "Who will help us against the might of God if it comes upon us" — meaning against the punishment of God, warning them of His vengeance if Musa was truthful. He reminded and warned, so Pharaoh knew that his proof had become manifest, and he said: "I show you only what I see." Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: I counsel you only with what I see for myself. "And I guide you only to the path of right conduct" — in denying Musa and believing in me.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And the one who believed said: O my people﴾ — he added to them in admonition: "Indeed I fear for you the like of the day of the factions," meaning the days of punishment in which those who banded together against the aforementioned prophets were punished.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿O my people, indeed I fear for you the day of calling out﴾ — he increased the admonition and warning and openly declared his faith, either submitting, preparing himself for being killed, or confident that they did not intend him harm; and God protected him from their evil by His true word: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed﴾. The reading of the common people is "al-Tanad" with the dal lightened, and it is the Day of Resurrection. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"He spread the creation within it when He spread it out... they are its inhabitants until the tanad."

It was named so because people call out to one another: the people of the heights (al-A'raf) call to men they recognise by their marks; the people of Paradise call to the people of the Fire: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true"; the people of the Fire call to the people of Paradise: "Pour upon us some of the water." A caller also calls out concerning wretchedness and happiness: "Indeed so-and-so son of so-and-so has become wretched with a wretchedness after which he will never be happy; indeed so-and-so son of so-and-so has become happy with a happiness after which he will never be wretched forever." This is at the weighing of deeds. The angels call to the people of Paradise: ﴿That is the Paradise you have been made to inherit for what you used to do﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]. And it is called out when Death is slaughtered: "O people of Paradise, eternity without death; O people of the Fire, eternity without death." And every people is called with their leader, and other calls besides these.

Al-Hasan, Ibn al-Sumayfa', Ya'qub, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid read "al-tanad" with the ya' affirmed in both pause and continuation, in accordance with the original form. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ikrimah read "yawma al-tanad" with the dal doubled. Some grammarians said: this is a lahn (solecism), because it derives from nadda yanidda, when one runs off fleeing headlong, as the poet said [[It is Tarafa. In al-Lisan: nawadihi amshi. He says: camels couched and sleeping, and their nawadi, meaning what fled from them. It is also narrated as hawadihi, meaning their first ones. That is, the fear of me stirred the nawadi of this couched herd as I walked toward it with a sword.]]:

"And a couched herd of sleeping camels, whose fleeing ones stirred my fear; I hasten with a drawn, keen sword."

He said: there is no sense in this regarding the Resurrection. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: this is an error, and the reading with it is sound, in the sense of the day of mutual repulsion (al-tanafur). Al-Dahhak said: that is when they hear the roaring of Hell, they flee in terror, but they do not reach any region of the earth without finding ranks of angels, so they return to the place where they were; this is His saying: "the day of the fleeing." And His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], and His saying: ﴿and the angel will be upon its borders﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17]. Ibn al-Mubarak reported it with this meaning. He said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir informed us, saying: Abd al-Jabbar ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Salman narrated to us concerning His saying: "Indeed I fear for you the day of calling out. The day you turn back fleeing..." then their eyes respond to them with tears, so they weep until the tears are exhausted; then their eyes respond to them with blood, so they weep until the blood is exhausted; then their eyes respond to them with pus. He said: a command from God is sent upon them and they turn back fleeing; then their eyes respond to them with pus, so they weep until the pus is exhausted, and their eyes sink like holes in mud.

It was also said that this occurs at the blowing of Israfil, peace be upon him, into the Trumpet, the blast of terror. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Ma'bad, al-Tabari and others from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, in which it says: the earth will be like a ship on the sea, struck by the waves, so people will sway upon its back; nursing mothers will be distracted, pregnant women will drop what is in their wombs, children will turn grey, and the devils will scatter fleeing, but the angels will meet them and strike their faces, and people will turn back fleeing, calling to one another. This is the day of which God, may He be exalted, says: "The day of calling out, the day you turn back fleeing; you have no protector from God; and whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide." The hadith in full. We have mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkirah and discussed it there.

It is narrated from Ali ibn Nasr from Abu Amr that the dal of "al-tanad" is sukun only in continuation. Abu Ma'mar narrated from Abd al-Warith the addition of the ya' only in continuation, and this is the school of Warsh. The well-known reading from Abu Amr is omitting it in both states. Likewise the rest of the seven read it, apart from Warsh according to what we mentioned from him, and apart from Ibn Kathir according to what preceded.

It was also said: the Day of Resurrection was named the Day of Calling Out because the disbeliever is called out to therein with woe, destruction and regret. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

It was also said: there is an ellipsis, meaning: "Indeed I fear for you the punishment of the Day of Calling Out." God knows best.

"The day you turn back fleeing" is in apposition to "the day of calling out." "And whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide": meaning, whoever God has placed misguidance in his heart, there is no guide for him. Regarding the speaker of these words there are two opinions: one is Musa; the second is the believer of the family of Pharaoh, and this is the more evident. And God knows best.

**The Lord's words: ﴿And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾.** It is said that this is part of the words of Moses. It is also said that it is part of the admonition of the believer from the family of Pharaoh, who reminded them of their ancient arrogance toward the prophets, and that he meant Joseph son of Jacob, who came to them with clear proofs. ﴿Are separate lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Yusuf: 39]

Ibn Juraij said: He was Joseph son of Jacob, whom God sent as a messenger to the Copts after the death of the king, before Moses, with clear proofs, which were dreams. Ibn Abbas said: He was Joseph son of Ephraim son of Joseph son of Jacob, who remained among them as a prophet for twenty years. Al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Dahhak that God sent to them a messenger from the jinn called Joseph. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The Pharaoh of Moses was the Pharaoh of Joseph, who lived a long life. Others say he was another.

Al-Nahhas said: Nothing in the verse indicates that it was him, because when a prophet brings clear proofs to those with him and to those after him, he has come to all of them with them, and they are obliged to believe him through them. ﴿You remained in doubt about what he brought you.﴾ That is, your forefathers were in doubt. ﴿Until, when he perished, you said: God will never send after him a messenger.﴾ That is, anyone who claims prophethood. ﴿Thus God leaves astray﴾ that is, in the same manner of that error, ﴿God leaves astray whoever is a transgressor﴾ (mushrik, one who associates partners with God), ﴿a doubter﴾ (shakk, one who doubts the Oneness of God, exalted is He).

**The Lord's words: ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of God﴾**, that is, concerning His manifest proofs, ﴿without any authority﴾, that is, without any proof or evidence. The word ﴿those who﴾ is in the accusative position as a substitution (badal, apposition) for ﴿whoever﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, thus God leaves astray those who dispute concerning the signs of God, so ﴿those who﴾ is in the accusative. He said: It may also be in the nominative, meaning "they are those who," or as an inchoative (mubtada'), with the predicate being ﴿it is greatly hateful in hatred﴾.

Then it is said: This is from the words of the believer of the family of Pharaoh. It is also said: It is the beginning of an address from God, the Exalted. ﴿Hateful in hatred﴾ is in the accusative as an explanation (tamyiz). That is, their disputing is greatly hateful, like His saying: ﴿It is a great word﴾ [al-Kahf: 5]. The hatred of God, the Exalted, means His condemnation of them, His cursing of them, and His bringing down punishment upon them.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, just as God sealed the hearts of these disputants, ﴿thus God seals﴾, that is, He stamps, ﴿upon every heart of a proud tyrant﴾, so that it cannot understand right guidance and cannot accept the truth.

The reading of the majority is ﴿upon every heart of a proud one﴾, with the word "heart" in construct form with "proud." Abu Hatim and Abu Ubayd preferred this reading. There is an ellipsis in the sentence, and the meaning is: ﴿Thus God seals upon every heart﴾ of every ﴿proud tyrant﴾, so the second "every" is omitted because what indicates it has preceded. If the omission of "every" is not assumed, the meaning would not be correct, because it would mean that He seals the whole heart, and that is not the intended meaning. The meaning is rather that He seals the hearts of the proud tyrants, heart by heart. Among what indicates the omission of "every" is the verse of Abu Dawud [note: he is Jariya ibn al-Hajjaj al-Iyadi; it is also said his name was Handhala ibn al-Sharqi, and he lived in the era of Ka'b ibn Mamah al-Iyadi, who is proverbial for generosity. Source: al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara' by Ibn Qutaybah]:

*"Does every man you think is a man,*
*and a fire kindled at night is a fire?"*

He means: and every fire. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿upon the heart of every proud one﴾, and this is a reading by way of explanation and construct. Abu Amr, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Dhakwan, from the people of Syria, read "qalbi" with tanwin (nunation), on the basis that "proud" is an adjective of "heart." Here the heart stands for the whole person, because the heart is what becomes proud and the other limbs follow it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart." It is also possible that this is by omitting a noun (idmar, ellipsis of a modifier), meaning "upon every one who has a proud heart," making the attribute belong to the possessor of the heart.
