Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verses 36–37:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Pharaoh said, "O Haman, build for me a tower"﴾. When the believer of Pharaoh's family (Mu'min Al Fir'awn) said what he said, and Pharaoh feared that the believer's words would take hold in the hearts of the people, he gave the impression that he was testing what Moses had brought of monotheism (tawhid). If its correctness became clear to him, he would not conceal it from them; and if it was not sound, he would keep them firm in their religion. So he ordered his minister Haman to build the tower (sarh). Its account has already passed in [al-Qasas [[See vol. 3, p. 288 and following, first or second edition.]]]. ﴿"That I may reach the causes, the causes of the heavens"﴾. "Asbab al-samawat" (the causes of the heavens) is a substitute (badal) for the first. The "asbab al-sama'" (causes of the sky) are, according to Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and al-Akhfash, its gates. He recited:

"And whoever fears the causes of death, they will reach him, even if he seeks the causes of the sky by a ladder."
[The verse is from the Mu'allaqa of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma.]

Abu Salih said: the causes of the heavens are their paths. It was also said: they are the means by which the heavens are held up. He repeated "asbab" for emphasis, because when a thing is made vague and then clarified, this magnifies its importance. And Allah knows best. ﴿"And that I may look at the God of Moses"﴾: that I may look at him with the gaze of one who overlooks him. He imagined that he was a body contained by places, and Pharaoh claimed divinity and thought its reality was established by sitting in an elevated place.

The reading of the common people is "fa-attali'a" (فَأَطَّلِعَ) with the nominative (raf'), coordinated (nasaq) with his saying "ablugh" (أَبْلُغُ). Al-A'raj, al-Sulami, Isa and Hafs read "fa-attali'a" with the accusative (nasb). Abu Ubayda said: it is in answer to "la'alla" (perhaps) with "fa" (then). Al-Nahhas said: the meaning of the accusative differs from the meaning of the nominative, because the meaning of the accusative is: when I reach the causes, I will look. The meaning of the nominative is: "perhaps I reach the causes," then "perhaps I look" after that; except that "thumma" (then) is more delayed than "fa."

﴿"And indeed I think him to be a liar"﴾: that is, indeed I think Moses is a liar in his claim of a god other than me, and I do what I do only to remove the doubt. This implies Pharaoh's doubt concerning the matter of Allah. It was also said: "zann" (ظَنّ, thought) here means "yaqin" (certainty), that is: and I am certain that he is a liar, and I say what I say only to remove doubt from those for whom I am not certain of what I am certain of.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus the evil of his deeds was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾, that is, polytheism and denial. ﴿"And he was barred from the way"﴾: the reading of the Kufans is "wa-ṣuddа" (وَصُدَّ) in the passive voice, which is the choice of Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim. It is permissible on this reading to read "wa-ṣiddа" (وَصِدَّ) with a kasra on the ṣad, the kasra of the dal being transferred to the ṣad; this is the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab and Alqama. Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abd al-Rahman ibn Bakra read "wa-ṣaddun ʿan al-sabil" (وَصَدٌّ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ) with the nominative and tanwin (nunation). The rest read "wa-ṣadda" (وَصَدَّ) with a fatha on the ṣad and the dal, meaning: Pharaoh barred the people from the way. ﴿"And the scheme of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin"﴾: that is, in loss and error. From the same root is ﴿"Perish the hands of Abu Lahab"﴾ [Al-Masad: 1], and His saying ﴿"they added nothing to them but ruin"﴾ [Hud: 101], and in another place ﴿"other than loss"﴾ [Hud: 63]. So Allah razed his tower, and drowned him and his people, as has already passed [[See vol. 13, p. 288 and following, first or second edition.]].

**The commentary on His words, Exalted is He:** ﴿And the one who believed said, "O my people, follow me."﴾ This is part of what the believer of Pharaoh's family said, meaning: take me as your example in the religion. ﴿I will guide you to the path of right guidance.﴾ That is, the way of guidance, which is Paradise. It has also been said that this is the speech of Musa (Moses).

Mu'adh ibn Jabal read *al-Rashad* with a shadda on the shin (*al-Rashshad*). Most grammarians (*ahl al-'Arabiyyah*) consider this a *lahn* (a grammatical error), because the verb is *arshada yurshidu*, and the form *fa''al* is not derived from *af'ala*; it comes from the triliteral root. If one wants intensification from the quadriliteral, one says *mif'al*. Al-Nahhas said: It is permissible that *rashshad* means *yurshid* without being derived from it, just as one says *la'ali'* (pearl-merchant) from *lu'lu'* (pearl), meaning the same thing without following its pattern. It is also permissible that *rashshad* is from *rashada yarshudu*, meaning "one possessing rashad," as the poet said:

*Kulini lahum ya Umaymatu nasibun*
(The verse is by al-Nabighah. Its complete form: *alladhdhu bayani*, and its continuation: "and a night I endure with the slow-moving stars.")

Al-Zamakhshari said: It has been read *al-Rashshad*, an intensive form (*fa''al*) from *rashida* (with kasra), like *'allam*, or from *rashada* (with fatha), like *'abbad*. It has also been said it is from *arshada*, like *jabbar* from *ajbar*, but this is not right, because *fa''al* from *af'ala* appears only in a few words, such as *dark*, *sar*, *qassar* and *jabbar*, and analogy cannot be based on this small set. It is also possible that it is a relative form from *al-rushd*, like *'awwaj* (ivory-seller) and *baththat* (seller of *bitt*, a thick cloak), without regard to any verb.

In the Mushaf (the written codex of the Qur'an), the word ﴿ittabi'una﴾ is written without a *ya'* (ي). Ya'qub and Ibn Kathir read it with the *ya'* both in continuation and at pause. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' drop it at pause but keep it in continuation, except Warsh, who drops it in both states, as do the rest, because it is written without a *ya'* in the Mushaf. Whoever keeps it does so according to the original form.

**His words, Exalted is He:** ﴿O my people, this worldly life is but a [temporary] enjoyment.﴾ That is, it is enjoyed for a little while, then it ends and passes away. ﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence.﴾ That is, the place of settled residence and eternity. By "the Hereafter abode" he means Paradise and Hell, because they do not perish. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 45–46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾, meaning from their inflicting various kinds of punishment upon him. They sought him but did not find him, because he had entrusted his affair to Allah. Qatadah said: he was a Copt, and Allah saved him along with the Children of Israel. According to this, the pronoun refers to the believer of Pharaoh's family. It was also said that it refers to Musa, according to the difference of opinion mentioned earlier. ﴿And there encompassed the people of Pharaoh the worst of the punishment﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: it is said "haqa yahiqu haqan and haywukan" when it descends and becomes binding. Then He clarified the punishment, saying: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it﴾. In this there are six aspects. It may be in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for "su'" (evil). It may mean "it is the Fire." It may be nominative as a beginning (mubtada'). Al-Farra' said: it may be nominative by the returning pronoun, meaning "the Fire, upon it they are exposed." These are four aspects in the nominative. Al-Farra' permitted the accusative, because after it there is a returning pronoun and before it there is what connects to it. Al-Akhfash permitted the genitive as a substitute for "al-adhab" (the punishment). The majority hold that this exposure is in the barzakh (intermediate state). Some scholars of knowledge used, in establishing the punishment of the grave, His saying: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, as long as the world lasts. Thus said Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Muqatil and Muhammad ibn Ka'b, all of them saying: this verse indicates the punishment of the grave in this world. Do you not see that He says concerning the punishment of the Hereafter: ﴿And on the day the Hour arises: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment."﴾ And in a hadith from Ibn Mas'ud: that the spirits of the people of Pharaoh and whoever was like them among the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, and it is said, "This is your abode." And also from him: their spirits are in the crops of black birds that go out to Jahannam and return twice every day, and that is its exposure. Shu'bah related from Ya'la ibn 'Ata', who said: I heard Maymun ibn Mihran [[In the manuscripts of the original: Maymun ibn Maysarah, which is an error; the correction is from "al-Tahdhib".]] say: Abu Hurayrah, when he entered the morning, would call out: "We have entered the morning, and praise be to Allah, and the people of Pharaoh have been exposed to the Fire." And when he entered the evening, he would call: "We have entered the evening, and praise be to Allah, and the people of Pharaoh have been exposed to the Fire." No one heard Abu Hurayrah without seeking refuge in Allah from the Fire. In the hadith of Sakhr ibn Juwayriyah from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the disbeliever dies, he is exposed to the Fire morning and evening." Then he recited: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾. "And when the believer dies, his spirit is exposed to Paradise morning and evening." Al-Bukhari and Muslim also reported from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When any one of you dies, his seat is shown to him morning and evening; if he is among the people of Paradise, then from the people of Paradise, and if he is among the people of the Fire, then from the people of the Fire. It is said to him, 'This is your seat, until Allah raises you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'" Al-Farra' said: "In the morning and evening" refers to measures of that in this world, and this is the view of Mujahid. He said: "morning and evening" means from the days of this world. Hammad ibn Muhammad al-Fazari said: A man said to al-Awza'i: "We have seen birds coming out of the sea, heading toward the west, white and small, in flocks, whose number none knows but Allah; then when evening comes they return like them but black." He said: "Those birds have in their crops the spirits of the people of Pharaoh, who are exposed to the Fire morning and evening; then they return to their nests, their feathers burnt and turned black, and then at night their feathers grow white again and the black ones fall off; then they go out in the morning and are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, then they return to their nest. That is their practice for as long as they were in this world. When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah, exalted is He, will say: ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment﴾," and that is the Hawiyah. Al-Awza'i said: We have been told that they were two million and six hundred thousand. And "morning" (ghuduwwan) is a verbal noun used as an adverb of time by extension, and "evening" ('ashiyyan) is conjoined to it, and the sentence is complete. Then one begins anew with ﴿and on the day the Hour arises﴾, on the basis that you put "yawm" in the accusative by His saying "admit." It may also be accusative by "they are exposed," meaning "they are exposed to the Fire in the world," and then ﴿and on the day the Hour arises﴾ is not a place to stop. Nafi' and the people of Madinah, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "adkhilu" with a hamzah of cutting and a kasrah on the kha' from "adkhil," and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, meaning He commands the angels to admit them, and its evidence is ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it﴾. The rest read "adkhilu" with a hamzah of connection and a dammah on the kha' from "dakhala," meaning it is said to them, "Enter, O people of Pharaoh, to the severest punishment," and this is the choice of Abu Hatim. He said: In the first reading, "al" is the first object and "ashadda" is the second object with the preposition elided; in the second reading it is accusative because it is a vocative construction with an annexed noun. The people of Pharaoh are whoever held his religion and his way; and when whoever held his religion and his way is in the severest punishment, he is closest to that. Ibn Mas'ud related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The servant is born a believer, lives a believer, and dies a believer; among them is Yahya ibn Zakariyya, who was born a believer, lived a believer, and died a believer. And the servant is born a disbeliever, lives a disbeliever, and dies a disbeliever; among them is Pharaoh, who was born a disbeliever, lived a disbeliever, and died a disbeliever." Mentioned by al-Nahhas. Al-Farra' made in the verse an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its meaning being: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment," and "The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening," so he made the exposure in the Hereafter, and this is contrary to what the majority held, that the discourse is coherent in its own sequence as already mentioned. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 47–50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they dispute with one another in the Fire﴾, i.e., they contend with each other therein. "Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant" regarding submission to the Prophets, "Indeed, we were to you followers" in what you called us to of polytheism in the world, "so will you relieve us of a portion of the Fire?" i.e., will you bear for us a share of the punishment? And the word "tabi'" (followers) is used as singular and as plural according to the Basran grammarians, its singular being "tabi'." The Kufan grammarians said: it is a plural with no singular, like the verbal noun, which is why it is not pluralized; had it been pluralized it would have been said "atba'." Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 51–54:

Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾. It is permissible to elide the damma (the short vowel "u") from "rusulana" because it is heavy, so it is said "rusulana" (with the damma dropped). The intended one is Musa (peace be upon him). "And those who believed in the life of this world" is in the accusative position, conjoined to "the messengers." The intended one is the believer who gave counsel. It was also said: it is general, covering the messengers and the believers, and their victory is by elevating the proofs and making them prevail, according to the view of Abu al-'Aliyah. It was also said: it is by taking vengeance upon their enemies. Al-Suddi said: No people ever killed a prophet, or a group of the callers to truth among the believers, except that Allah, mighty and majestic, sent someone who would avenge them, so they became victorious in this world even though they were killed.

Allah's saying: ﴿And the day when the witnesses will stand﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. Zayd ibn Aslam said: "al-ashhad" (the witnesses) are four: the angels, the prophets, the believers, and the limbs. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "al-ashhad" are the angels, who testify for the prophets that they conveyed the message, and against the nations that they denied it. Qatadah said: the angels and the prophets. Then it was said: "al-ashhad" is the plural of "shahid" (witness), like "sharif" and "ashraf." Al-Zajjaj said: "al-ashhad" is the plural of "shahid," like "sahib" and "ashab." Al-Nahhas said: the pattern "fa'il" is not regularly pluralized on the pattern "af'al," and it is not analogized upon; rather, whatever of it comes transmitted is reported as it was heard, and it was on the basis of dropping the extra letter. Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' permitted "wa-yawma taqumu al-ashhad" with the ta' (feminine form), on the grounds of the feminine gender of the collective noun. And in a hadith from Abu al-Darda', some narrators say, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Whoever defends the honour of his Muslim brother, it is a right upon Allah, mighty and majestic, that He will ward off the Fire of Jahannam from him." Then he recited: "Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believed." And from him (peace be upon him) that he said: "Whoever protects a believer from a hypocrite who backbites him, Allah, mighty and majestic, will send on the Day of Resurrection an angel to protect him from the Fire; and whoever mentions a Muslim with something that disgraces him, Allah, mighty and majestic, will halt him upon a bridge of Jahannam until he comes out of what he said." "And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book": meaning the Torah, which We made an inheritance for them. "A guidance" is a substitute for "the Book," and it may also be read as meaning "it is a guidance," that is, that Book. "And a reminder for people of understanding": that is, an admonition for possessors of intellect.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 40, verses 55–59:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾. That is: so be patient, O Muhammad, over the harm of the polytheists, as those before you were patient. "Indeed, the promise of Allah is true" refers to His support for you and the manifestation of your cause, just as He supported Musa and the Children of Israel. Al-Kalbi said: this was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

"And ask forgiveness for your sin." It has been said: this means for the sin of your community, the genitive-governing noun (al-mudaf) being omitted and the noun in the genitive (al-mudaf ilayhi) put in its place. It has also been said: it means for your own sin, according to those who permit minor sins (al-saghair) in the case of the prophets. Whoever says that it is not permissible says: this is an act of worship (ta'abbud) for the Prophet (peace be upon him) through supplication, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And grant us what You promised us﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 194]. The benefit is an increase in ranks and that the supplication becomes a practice (sunnah) for those who come after him. It has also been said: "so seek forgiveness of Allah" for a sin that proceeded from you before prophethood.

"And glorify your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning." This means the Fajr prayer and the 'Asr prayer, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah. It has also been said that it refers to a prayer that was performed in Makkah before the five daily prayers were made obligatory: two rak'ahs in the morning and two rak'ahs in the evening. This is also from al-Hasan, as reported by al-Mawardi. Thus this would be among what was abrogated, and Allah knows best.

His saying "with the praise of your Lord" means with thanks to Him and praise of Him. It has also been said: "glorify with the praise of your Lord" means continue the glorification (tasbih) during the prayer and outside it, so that you occupy yourself with that rather than with hastening the victory.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who dispute﴾, that is, they argue "concerning the signs of Allah without authority" (sultan), meaning without proof, "having come to them. There is nothing in their breasts except pride, which they will never attain." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that there is nothing in their breasts except pride, which they will not attain in their aspiration, and the phrase is constructed with an omission (hadhf). Others said: the meaning is that they will never reach the greatness (al-kibr) without any omission, because these people reasoned that if they followed the Prophet (peace be upon him) their status would diminish and their conditions would decline, while if they were not followers they would rise. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed them that they will not reach the elevation they hoped for through denial. The intended people are the polytheists. It has also been said they are the Jews, and on this view the verse is Madani, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surahs.

The meaning is: if you are arrogant about following Muhammad (peace be upon him), and they say that the Dajjal (Antichrist) will emerge soon and return the kingdom to us, and rivers will flow with him, and he is one of the signs of Allah, then that is a pride they will not attain. So the verse was revealed concerning them. Abu al-'Aliyah and others said this. It has already been mentioned in Ali 'Imran that he will emerge and trample all the lands except Makkah and Madinah. We have mentioned his report in full in the book al-Tadhkirah. He is a Jew, his name is Safi, and he is called Abu Yusuf. It has also been said that the verse refers to everyone who disbelieved in the Prophet (peace be upon him). This is a good view, because it is general. Mujahid said: its meaning is that there is greatness in their breasts which they will not attain, and the meaning is one and the same. It has also been said that by pride is meant a great matter, that is, they seek prophethood, or a great matter by which they would reach you, such as killing and the like, but they will not reach it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾. It has been said: from the trial of the Dajjal, according to the view of those who say the verse was revealed about the Jews. And according to the other view, from the evil of the disbelievers. It has been said: from the likeness of what they were tested with, namely disbelief and pride. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. The word "huwa" (He) may serve as a separator (fasil), or it may be a subject (mubtada') with what follows it as its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), as explained above.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾. The phrase is a subject (mubtada') and its predicate. Abu al-'Aliyah said: that is, greater than the creation of the Dajjal, when the Jews magnified him. Yahya ibn Sallam said: this is an argument against those who deny the resurrection, meaning that the heavens and the earth are greater than the re-creation of mankind, so why do they believe that I am incapable of it? ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾ that.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And not equal are the blind and the seeing﴾, that is, the believer and the disbeliever, the astray and the guided. ﴿Nor those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, that is, the doer of righteous deeds is not equal to ﴿nor the wrongdoer﴾ who does evil deeds. ﴿Little do you remember﴾. The reading of the majority is with the letter ya' (the third person, as a report), and this was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because of the report before it and after it. The Kufans read it with the letter ta' (the second person, as direct address).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾. This is the emphatic lam (lam al-ta'kid), which entered the predicate of "inna." Its proper place is at the beginning of the sentence, since it emphasizes the clause, but it is shifted from its position, as Sibawayh said. You say: "Inna 'Umar la-kharijun" (Indeed, 'Umar is surely going out). It was delayed from its place so that it would not be combined with "inna," because both serve the same meaning. Likewise, according to the Basrans, "inna" and "anna" are not combined. Hisham permitted "inna anna Zaydan munṭaliqun haqqun" (indeed that Zayd is departing is true). If you omit "haqqan" (true), no grammarian permits it, as far as I know, as al-Nahhas reported. ﴿There is no doubt concerning it﴾, that is, no uncertainty and no dispute. ﴿But most of mankind do not believe﴾, that is, they do not affirm it. And it is at that point that the difference between the obedient and the disobedient becomes clear.

**Al-Qurtubi's Commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 40, Verses 60–65**

Allah's words: ﴿And your Lord says: "Call upon Me, I will respond to you."﴾ (to the end of the verse). Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir narrated: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Supplication (du'a') is worship." Then he recited: ﴿And your Lord says: "Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated."﴾ Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hadith that is hasan sahih (good and sound). This indicates that supplication is worship. Most of the commentators (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir) also said this, and the meaning is: "Affirm My oneness and worship Me, and I will accept your worship and forgive you." It was also said: it means remembrance (dhikr), supplication (du'a') and asking (su'al). Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let each of you ask his Lord for all his needs, even asking Him for the strap of his sandal when it breaks." It is also said that supplication means abandoning sins. Qatadah related that Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "This Ummah has been given three things that no nation before them was given, except for a prophet: when a prophet was sent, it was said to him, 'You are a witness over your nation,' and Allah said to this Ummah: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. It was said to the Prophet: ﴿He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾, and to this Ummah He said: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. It was said to the Prophet: 'Call upon Me and I will respond to you,' and to this Ummah He said: 'Call upon Me, I will respond to you.'" I (al-Qurtubi) say: Such a thing is not said on the basis of opinion (ra'y). It has also come as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report, narrated by Layth from Shahr ibn Hawshab from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "My Ummah has been given three things that were given only to the prophets. When Allah sent a prophet, He said to him, 'Call upon Me and I will respond to you,' and He said to this Ummah, 'Call upon Me, I will respond to you.' And when Allah sent a prophet, He said, 'He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion,' and He said to this Ummah, ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. And when Allah sent a prophet, He made him a witness over his people, and He made this Ummah witnesses over mankind." This was recorded by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul. Khalid al-Rab'i used to say: "How wonderful this Ummah is! It was told: 'Call upon Me, I will respond to you.' He commanded them to supplicate and promised them a response, with no condition between them." Someone said to him: "Like what?" He said: "Like His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25], where there is a condition. And His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe that they will have a sure place of honour with their Lord﴾ [Yunus: 2], which has no condition of action. And like His saying: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir: 14], where there is a condition. But His saying: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ has no condition." The community used to turn to their prophets for their needs, until the prophets would ask (Allah) on their behalf. It has been said: this is from the category of the absolute (mutlaq) and the restricted (muqayyad), as was explained earlier in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 309, second edition], and its explanation is: "I will respond to you" if I wish, like His saying: ﴿He will remove that which you call upon Him for, if He wills﴾ [al-An'am: 41]. The response may also be other than the exact thing requested, according to the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, as was explained earlier in al-Baqarah, so reflect on it there.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Ruways from Ya'qub, Ayyash from Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read ﴿sayudkhalun﴾ (with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the khā', in the passive voice, the subject not named). The rest read ﴿yadkhulun﴾ (with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the khā'). The meaning of ﴿dakhirin﴾ is: humbled, abased. This has been mentioned previously [see vol. 10, p. 111, and vol. 13, p. 242, first or second edition].

Allah's words: ﴿It is Allah who made the night for you to rest therein﴾. The word "ja'ala" (made) here means "khalaqa" (created). The Arabs distinguish between "ja'ala" when it means "khalaqa" and "ja'ala" when it does not. When it means "khalaqa," it takes only one object; when it does not, it takes two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3]. This meaning has been discussed before [see vol. 6, p. 386 onwards, first or second edition]. ﴿And the day giving sight﴾ means: illuminated, so that you can see your needs therein and go about seeking your livelihood. ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ for His favour and bounty upon them. This shows the evidence of His oneness and power. ﴿There is no deity except Him, so how are you deluded?﴾ That is: how do you turn back and turn away from belief after its evidences have become clear to you? Just as you were turned away from the truth despite the existence of the proof for it. So ﴿thus are deluded﴾ means: turned away from the truth, ﴿those who used to deny the signs of Allah﴾.

Allah's words: ﴿It is Allah who made the earth for you as a place of settlement﴾. This adds emphasis to the definition and the proof, meaning: He made the earth a settled place for you in your life and after death. ﴿And the sky as a canopy﴾ has been mentioned previously [see vol. 1, p. 229, second or third edition]. ﴿And He formed you and perfected your forms﴾ means: He created you in the best form. Abu Razin and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read ﴿ṣiwarakum﴾ with a kasrah on the ṣād. Al-Jawhari said: "al-ṣiwar," with a kasrah on the ṣād, is a dialectal variant of "al-ṣuwar," the plural of "ṣurah" (form). This line of verse is recited in this dialect, describing female slave-girls:

Their eyes resemble those of the cows of al-Khalsa'
They are more beautiful than their herds in form.

"Al-ṣiyaran" is the plural of "ṣiwar," which means a herd of cattle; "al-ṣiwar" also means a musk-bag. The poet combined both meanings in his saying:

When the ṣiwar (herd) appears, I remember Layla,
And I remember her when the ṣiwar (musk-bag) is blown.

"Al-ṣiyar" is also a dialectal form of it. ﴿And provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord. So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾ has been mentioned previously [see vol. 7, p. 223, first or second edition; and vol. 1, p. 136, second or third edition]. ﴿He is the Living; there is no deity except Him, so invoke Him, sincere to Him in religion﴾ means: the Ever-Living who does not die. The "religion" means obedience and worship. ﴿Praise is to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is a statement (khabar) with an implied command, meaning: "Invoke Him and praise Him." All of this has been fully discussed before in al-Baqarah [the author discussed this in his commentary on al-Fatihah, vol. 1, p. 136; so refer to it there, not to al-Baqarah; perhaps the original text contains an error], and in other places. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever says "There is no deity but Allah," let him then say "Praise is to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

This adds emphasis to the definition and the proof, meaning: He made the earth a settled place for you in your life and after death. ﴿And the sky as a canopy﴾ has been mentioned previously [see vol. 1, p. 229, second or third edition]. ﴿And He formed you and perfected your forms﴾ means: He created you in the best form. Abu Razin and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read ﴿ṣiwarakum﴾ with a kasrah on the ṣād. Al-Jawhari said: "al-ṣiwar," with a kasrah on the ṣād, is a dialectal variant of "al-ṣuwar," the plural of "ṣurah" (form). This line of verse is recited in this dialect, describing female slave-girls:

Their eyes resemble those of the cows of al-Khalsa'
They are more beautiful than their herds in form.

"Al-ṣiyaran" is the plural of "ṣiwar," which means a herd of cattle; "al-ṣiwar" also means a musk-bag. The poet combined both meanings in his saying:

When the ṣiwar (herd) appears, I remember Layla,
And I remember her when the ṣiwar (musk-bag) is blown.

"Al-ṣiyar" is also a dialectal form of it. ﴿And provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord. So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾ has been mentioned previously [see vol. 7, p. 223, first or second edition; and vol. 1, p. 136, second or third edition]. ﴿He is the Living; there is no deity except Him, so invoke Him, sincere to Him in religion﴾ means: the Ever-Living who does not die. The "religion" means obedience and worship. ﴿Praise is to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is a statement (khabar) with an implied command, meaning: "Invoke Him and praise Him." All of this has been fully discussed before in al-Baqarah [the author discussed this in his commentary on al-Fatihah, vol. 1, p. 136; so refer to it there, not to al-Baqarah; perhaps the original text contains an error], and in other places. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever says "There is no deity but Allah," let him then say "Praise is to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 66–68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Indeed I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah, when the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord, and I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ That is, say, O Muhammad: Allah has forbidden me, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and there is no god but Him, "to worship" other than Him, "when the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord," that is, the evidences of His oneness, "and I have been commanded to submit," to humble myself and be obedient, "to the Lord of the worlds." They had invited him to the religion of his forefathers, so he was commanded to say this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot, then He brings you forth as a child﴾, that is, as children. This has already been mentioned [see vol. 12, p. 11 ff., first or second edition]. ﴿Then that you may reach your maturity﴾, which is the state of gathered strength and complete intellect. Its explanation has already passed in [al-An'am]. ﴿Then that you may become elders﴾. Reading with a dammah on the shin (shuyukhan) is the recitation of Nafi', Ibn Muhaysin, Hafs, Hisham, Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr, according to the original form, since it is the plural of fa'l, like qalb and qulub, ra's and ru'us. The rest read with a kasrah on the shin (shiyukhan), out of regard for the ya', and both are plurals of abundance (jam' kathrah). In the paucity plural (jam' qillah) one says ashyakh, and the original is ashyukh, like fals and afluss, except that the movement on the ya' is heavy. It is also read shaykhan in the singular, as in His saying "tiflan" (a child), meaning each one of you, and the singular was used because the purpose is to explain the category. In al-Sihah: the plural of shaykh is shuyukh, ashyakh, shaykhah, shaykhan, mashyakhah, mashayikh and mashyukha'. A woman is shaykhah. ʿUbayd [that is, ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras] said:

"As if she were an aged mother, a barren one who watches over her child, lest it die."
[The rquub is one who watches her child fearing it may die. The verse describes his horse, and its completion is: "She spent the night upon a hill, soft..."]

The man has grown old (shakha yashikhu shaykhan, with vowelling on its original form, and shaykhukhah). The original of the ya' is vowelled, then it was made sukun, because there is no fa'ulun pattern in the language. Shayyakha tashyikhan means shakha (he grew old). Shayyakhtuhu (the addition is from the lexicons) means I called him shaykh as a mark of honour. The diminutive of shaykh is shuyayk and shiyayk, also with a kasrah on the shin, and one should not say shuwayk. Al-Nahhas said: if a poet is compelled, it is permissible for him to say ashyukh, like ʿayn and aʿyun, but it is better with ʿayn, because it is feminine. A shaykh is one who has passed forty years. ﴿And among you is one who dies before﴾. Mujahid said: that is, before becoming a shaykh, or before these stages, if he is expelled as a miscarriage. ﴿And that you may reach an appointed term﴾. Mujahid said: death, for all. The lam is the lam of consequence. ﴿And perhaps you will reason﴾, so that you may know that there is no god but Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death﴾. He added in the tanbih (emphasis), that is, He is the One who is able to give life and cause death. ﴿And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ That is, when He wills its doing, He says to it, "Be," and it is. Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿fayakuna﴾ in the accusative as a response to the imperative. It has already been discussed in [al-Baqarah].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 69–78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah? How are they turned away?﴾ Ibn Zayd said: They are the polytheists, by the evidence of His saying: "Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers." Most of the exegetes said: It was revealed concerning the Qadariyya. Ibn Sirin said: If this verse was not revealed concerning the Qadariyya, then I do not know concerning whom it was revealed. Abu Qabil said: I do not reckon the deniers of predestination (al-qadar) except those who dispute with the believers. Uqba ibn Amir said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This verse was revealed concerning the Qadariyya." Al-Mahdawi narrated it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾ means: soon they will know the falsehood of what they are in when they enter the Fire, and their hands will be chained to their necks. Al-Taymi said: If one shackle of the shackles of Hell were placed upon a mountain, it would crush it until it reached the black water. "And the chains" with the nominative is the reading of the common readers, in conjunction with "the shackles." Abu Hatim said: "they are dragged" is a new (independent) clause according to this reading. Others said: it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the implied meaning is: "When the shackles are around their necks and the chains" [they are] being dragged. Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Jawza, Ikrima and Ibn Mas'ud read "and the chains" with the accusative and "they are dragged" with an open ya', and the implied meaning in this reading is "and they drag the chains." Ibn Abbas said: When they drag them, it is more severe for them. It is related from some of them "and the chains" with the genitive, and its basis is that it is construed according to the meaning, because the meaning is "their necks are in the shackles and the chains," as al-Farra' said. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "and the chains, they are dragged" with the genitive, the meaning according to him is "and in the chains they are dragged." Ibn al-Anbari said: The genitive on this meaning is not permissible, because when you say "Zayd is in the house," it is not good to omit "in" and say "Zayd the house"; but the genitive is permissible in the sense of "when their necks are in the shackles and the chains," so you put the chains in the genitive by coordination with the reading of the shackles. The shackles are construed as genitive. It is also permissible to read them in the nominative, because when one of them disputes with his companion, his companion has also disputed with him. Al-Farra' recited:

Since the ancient ones made peace with the snakes from him, the al-Af'wan and the al-Shuja' al-Shajʿama [[al-Shajʿam: the large one among snakes.]]

So he put al-Af'wan in the accusative by following the snakes, since when the foot made peace with them, the foot has also made peace with them. Whoever puts "the chains" in the accusative or the genitive does not stop upon it. "Al-hamim" is the extremely hot water. It is said: it is boiling pus. ﴿Then in the Fire they are burned﴾ means they are cast into it and become its fuel; Mujahid said so. It is said: "I kindled the oven" meaning I lit it, and "I filled it" meaning I filled it; from this is ﴿and the sea that is filled (al-masjur)﴾ [al-Tur: 6], meaning filled. So the meaning according to this is: the Fire is filled with them. And the poet, describing a wild goat, said:

When it wills, it looks at a pool that is full, and it sees around it the nab' and the simsim

meaning a spring filled with water.

﴿Then it will be said to them: Where is that which you used to associate besides Allah?﴾ This is rebuke and reproach. ﴿They will say: They have departed from us﴾ meaning they have perished and gone away from us and left us in the punishment, from the phrase "the water got lost in the milk," meaning it became hidden. It was also said: meaning they have become such that we do not find them. ﴿Rather, we used not to call upon anything before﴾ meaning something that does not see, does not hear, and neither harms nor benefits. This is not a denial of the worship of idols; rather it is an acknowledgment that their worship of idols was false. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Thus does Allah lead astray the disbelievers﴾ meaning: just as He led these astray, He does the same to every disbeliever.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That﴾ meaning: that is the punishment ﴿because you used to exult﴾ in sins. It is said to them this as rebuke, meaning: this has befallen you only because of what you used to display in the world of joy in disobedience and abundance of wealth, followers and health. It was also said that their joy in it was that they said to the messengers: "We know that we will not be resurrected nor punished." Mujahid also said similarly regarding the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾ [Ghafir: 83]. ﴿And because you used to exult (tamrahun)﴾ Mujahid and others said: meaning you were insolent and arrogant. Its explanation has already passed in "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 260, first or second edition.]]. Al-Dahhak said: al-farah is joy, and al-maraḥ is transgression. Khalid narrated from Thawr from Mu'adh who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah hates the arrogant, joyful ones, and loves every sorrowful heart, and hates a people who are fleshy, and hates every fat scholar." As for "a people who are fleshy": they are those who eat the flesh of people through backbiting. As for "the fat scholar": he is the one who is proud of his knowledge and does not inform people of his knowledge, meaning one who hoards his knowledge and from whom people do not benefit. Mentioned by al-Mawardi. It has also been said regarding the "lahimin" that they are those who eat much meat; from this is the saying of Umar: "Beware of these slaughterhouses, for they have a craving like the craving of wine," mentioned by al-Mahdawi. The first is the saying of Sufyan al-Thawri. ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾ meaning it will be said to them that day, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿It has seven gates﴾ [al-Hijr: 44]. ﴿So evil is the abode of the arrogant﴾ — all of this has already passed [[See vol. 10, p. 30 and p. 100, first or second edition.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ This is consolation to the Prophet, peace be upon him, meaning: We will surely avenge you upon them, either during your lifetime or in the Hereafter. ﴿Whether We show you﴾ is in a position of conditional jussive, and "ma" is an added particle for emphasis, and likewise the nun; the jussive is removed and the verb is built on the fatha. ﴿Or We cause you to die﴾ is conjoined to it. ﴿Then to Us they will be returned﴾ is the response.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you﴾ He consoles him also with what the messengers before him encountered. ﴿Of them are those We have related to you﴾ meaning We have informed you of their accounts and what they encountered from their peoples. ﴿And of them are those We have not related to you. And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾ — he cannot bring it from his own self; rather it is from Allah, meaning not from his own self, ﴿except by permission of Allah. So when the command of Allah comes﴾ meaning when the appointed time of their punishment comes, Allah destroys them. The delay was only for the Islam of those whom Allah knew would embrace Islam among them, and for the believers in their loins. It was also said: He pointed by this to the killing at Badr. ﴿The matter will be decided between them with truth, and there will be lost there the falsifiers﴾ meaning those who follow falsehood and shirk.

How are they turned away?﴾ Ibn Zayd said: They are the polytheists, by the evidence of His saying: "Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers." Most of the exegetes said: It was revealed concerning the Qadariyya. Ibn Sirin said: If this verse was not revealed concerning the Qadariyya, then I do not know concerning whom it was revealed. Abu Qabil said: I do not reckon the deniers of predestination (al-qadar) except those who dispute with the believers. Uqba ibn Amir said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This verse was revealed concerning the Qadariyya." Al-Mahdawi narrated it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾ means: soon they will know the falsehood of what they are in when they enter the Fire, and their hands will be chained to their necks. Al-Taymi said: If one shackle of the shackles of Hell were placed upon a mountain, it would crush it until it reached the black water. "And the chains" with the nominative is the reading of the common readers, in conjunction with "the shackles." Abu Hatim said: "they are dragged" is a new (independent) clause according to this reading. Others said: it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the implied meaning is: "When the shackles are around their necks and the chains" [they are] being dragged. Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Jawza, Ikrima and Ibn Mas'ud read "and the chains" with the accusative and "they are dragged" with an open ya', and the implied meaning in this reading is "and they drag the chains." Ibn Abbas said: When they drag them, it is more severe for them. It is related from some of them "and the chains" with the genitive, and its basis is that it is construed according to the meaning, because the meaning is "their necks are in the shackles and the chains," as al-Farra' said. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "and the chains, they are dragged" with the genitive, the meaning according to him is "and in the chains they are dragged." Ibn al-Anbari said: The genitive on this meaning is not permissible, because when you say "Zayd is in the house," it is not good to omit "in" and say "Zayd the house"; but the genitive is permissible in the sense of "when their necks are in the shackles and the chains," so you put the chains in the genitive by coordination with the reading of the shackles. The shackles are construed as genitive. It is also permissible to read them in the nominative, because when one of them disputes with his companion, his companion has also disputed with him. Al-Farra' recited:

Since the ancient ones made peace with the snakes from him, the al-Af'wan and the al-Shuja' al-Shajʿama [[al-Shajʿam: the large one among snakes.]]

So he put al-Af'wan in the accusative by following the snakes, since when the foot made peace with them, the foot has also made peace with them. Whoever puts "the chains" in the accusative or the genitive does not stop upon it. "Al-hamim" is the extremely hot water. It is said: it is boiling pus. ﴿Then in the Fire they are burned﴾ means they are cast into it and become its fuel; Mujahid said so. It is said: "I kindled the oven" meaning I lit it, and "I filled it" meaning I filled it; from this is ﴿and the sea that is filled (al-masjur)﴾ [al-Tur: 6], meaning filled. So the meaning according to this is: the Fire is filled with them. And the poet, describing a wild goat, said:

When it wills, it looks at a pool that is full, and it sees around it the nab' and the simsim

meaning a spring filled with water.

﴿Then it will be said to them: Where is that which you used to associate besides Allah?﴾ This is rebuke and reproach. ﴿They will say: They have departed from us﴾ meaning they have perished and gone away from us and left us in the punishment, from the phrase "the water got lost in the milk," meaning it became hidden. It was also said: meaning they have become such that we do not find them. ﴿Rather, we used not to call upon anything before﴾ meaning something that does not see, does not hear, and neither harms nor benefits. This is not a denial of the worship of idols; rather it is an acknowledgment that their worship of idols was false. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Thus does Allah lead astray the disbelievers﴾ meaning: just as He led these astray, He does the same to every disbeliever.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That﴾ meaning: that is the punishment ﴿because you used to exult﴾ in sins. It is said to them this as rebuke, meaning: this has befallen you only because of what you used to display in the world of joy in disobedience and abundance of wealth, followers and health. It was also said that their joy in it was that they said to the messengers: "We know that we will not be resurrected nor punished." Mujahid also said similarly regarding the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾ [Ghafir: 83]. ﴿And because you used to exult (tamrahun)﴾ Mujahid and others said: meaning you were insolent and arrogant. Its explanation has already passed in "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 260, first or second edition.]]. Al-Dahhak said: al-farah is joy, and al-maraḥ is transgression. Khalid narrated from Thawr from Mu'adh who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah hates the arrogant, joyful ones, and loves every sorrowful heart, and hates a people who are fleshy, and hates every fat scholar." As for "a people who are fleshy": they are those who eat the flesh of people through backbiting. As for "the fat scholar": he is the one who is proud of his knowledge and does not inform people of his knowledge, meaning one who hoards his knowledge and from whom people do not benefit. Mentioned by al-Mawardi. It has also been said regarding the "lahimin" that they are those who eat much meat; from this is the saying of Umar: "Beware of these slaughterhouses, for they have a craving like the craving of wine," mentioned by al-Mahdawi. The first is the saying of Sufyan al-Thawri. ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾ meaning it will be said to them that day, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿It has seven gates﴾ [al-Hijr: 44]. ﴿So evil is the abode of the arrogant﴾ — all of this has already passed [[See vol. 10, p. 30 and p. 100, first or second edition.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ This is consolation to the Prophet, peace be upon him, meaning: We will surely avenge you upon them, either during your lifetime or in the Hereafter. ﴿Whether We show you﴾ is in a position of conditional jussive, and "ma" is an added particle for emphasis, and likewise the nun; the jussive is removed and the verb is built on the fatha. ﴿Or We cause you to die﴾ is conjoined to it. ﴿Then to Us they will be returned﴾ is the response.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you﴾ He consoles him also with what the messengers before him encountered. ﴿Of them are those We have related to you﴾ meaning We have informed you of their accounts and what they encountered from their peoples. ﴿And of them are those We have not related to you. And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾ — he cannot bring it from his own self; rather it is from Allah, meaning not from his own self, ﴿except by permission of Allah. So when the command of Allah comes﴾ meaning when the appointed time of their punishment comes, Allah destroys them. The delay was only for the Islam of those whom Allah knew would embrace Islam among them, and for the believers in their loins. It was also said: He pointed by this to the killing at Badr. ﴿The matter will be decided between them with truth, and there will be lost there the falsifiers﴾ meaning those who follow falsehood and shirk.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 79–81:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is Allah who made for you the cattle﴾. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: al-an'am here means the camels. ﴿That you may ride some of them and of them you eat﴾. Those who forbade eating horses and permitted eating camels argued that Allah, mighty and majestic, said of the cattle: "and of them you eat," and said of horses: ﴿And horses and mules and donkeys, for you to ride﴾ [al-Nahl: 8], and did not mention their being permitted for eating. This has been discussed fully before in "al-Nahl" [[See vol. 10, p. 96 onward, first or second edition.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for you in them are benefits﴾: in the wool, the fleece, the hair, the milk, the butter, the ghee, the cheese and other things. ﴿And that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾, i.e., they carry the burdens and the journeys. This whole matter has been explained before in "al-Nahl" [[See vol. 10, p. 71, first or second edition.]], so there is no point in repeating it. Then He said: ﴿And upon them, meaning the cattle on land, and upon the ship at sea, you are carried. He shows you His signs﴾.

That is, His signs which indicate His oneness and His power in what has been mentioned.

﴿Then which of Allah's signs will you deny?﴾

"Ayya" (which) is in the accusative governed by "tunkiruna" (you deny), because the interrogative has the front position in the sentence, so what precedes it does not govern it. If there were a pronoun with the verb, the preferred reading for "ayy" would be the nominative. And if the interrogative were with a hamza or "hal" and after them there was a noun followed by a verb with a pronoun, the preferred reading would be the accusative. That is: if you do not deny that these things are from Allah, then why do you deny His power over resurrection and raising up?

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 40, verse 82–85:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ So that they witness the traces of the earlier nations, "who were more numerous than them" in number, "and greater in strength and in monuments upon the earth, but what they earned did not avail them" of the buildings and wealth, and of the children and followers they relied upon. It is said: "I relied (dalawtu) upon so-and-so to you," meaning I sought his intercession with you. On this reading, "mā" is for negation, meaning that this availed them nothing. It was also said: "mā" is interrogative, meaning: what availed them their earnings when they perished? And "lam yanṣarif" is in the pattern of "af'al." The Kufans claimed that everything that is not declined (lā yanṣarif) may be declined, except "af'al" with "min," for it is not permissible to decline it in any way, in poetry or otherwise, when "min" accompanies it. Abu al-'Abbas said: If "min" were the preventive cause of its non-declension, it would be obligatory not to say: "I passed by someone better than you (khayrin minka) and worse than you (sharrin minka)" [[The addition is from I'rab al-Qur'an of al-Nahhas.]] and "min 'Amrin."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, that is, with clear signs. "They rejoiced in what knowledge they had" — there are three opinions regarding its meaning. Mujahid said: the disbelievers who rejoiced in the knowledge they had said: "We are more knowledgeable than them; we will not be punished and we will not be resurrected." It was also said: the disbelievers rejoiced in their worldly knowledge, like ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ [al-Rum: 7]. It was also said: those who rejoiced were the messengers; when their people denied them, Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed them that He would destroy the disbelievers and save them and the believers, so "they rejoiced in what knowledge they had" regarding the salvation of the believers. "And there befell them" — that is, the disbelievers — "what they used to mock at," meaning the punishment for their mockery of what the messengers, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, brought.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then when they saw Our might﴾, that is, they witnessed the punishment. "They said: We believe in Allah alone, and we reject what we used to associate with Him" — that is, the idols which we associated with Him in worship. "But their faith did not benefit them" in Allah when they witnessed the punishment and at the time they saw the might. "The way (sunnata) of Allah" is a verbal noun, because the Arabs say: sanna yasunnu sannan and sunnatan, meaning Allah the Mighty and Majestic established (sanna) regarding the disbelievers that faith does not benefit them when they see the punishment. This has been explained above in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5 p. 92 and following, first or second edition.]] and "Yunus" [[See vol. 8 p. 384, first or second edition.]], and that repentance is not accepted after seeing the punishment and the attainment of necessary knowledge. It was also said: meaning, be wary, O people of Makkah, of the way of Allah in destroying the disbelievers; so "sunnata Allah" is in the accusative by way of warning and incitement. ﴿And there the disbelievers were lost﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: they had been losers before that, but He made the loss clear to us when they saw the punishment. It was also said: there is inversion in it, meaning: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might, and there the disbelievers were lost﴾, like Our way regarding all disbelievers; so "sunnata" is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: like the way of Allah among all the nations. And Allah knows best. Then the tafsir of Surah "Ghafir" — and praise be to Allah.

And Allah knows best. Then the tafsir of Surah "Ghafir" — and praise be to Allah.
